A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, architecture, algorithm and CompoSuite study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison. v1 Appendix A is retained in v4 Section 4.7.1, and implementation details move from Appendix B to Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original CompoSuite simulation results, including policy success rates, iterative generation, intervention and attention analyses, and a training-task-count study in Appendix A.

after.justification: v4 retains these results and adds online-RL comparisons, further iterative-generation analyses, multi-robot iterative results and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The factor-specific encoder-decoder architecture, task conditioning, diffusion objective and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. New downstream online-RL experiments evaluate generated data without revising the proposed generation procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CompoSuite task families and expert data. The four-robot, 256-task space was already evaluated in v1 Appendix A, and the IIWA task lists are identical. v4 adds iterative and online-learning evaluations within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: v4 adds RLPD as an evaluated offline-to-online comparator in Section 4.5 and compares synthetic-data-initialized RLPD against SAC from scratch in Section 4.6. SAC previously appeared as dataset-generation background, not an evaluated comparator. The original offline-RL and generative baselines remain.

E3.justification: v4 adds raw per-iteration success and admitted-dataset coverage metrics, iterative evaluation in the 56/256 regime, and online-learning protocols. These include 100,000-step RLPD runs and two selected low-success cases with 500,000-step RLPD versus 5,000,000-step SAC budgets. Original settings in Tables 1–5 are unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether improvement survives replacing best-so-far aggregation, distinguish occasional task success from dataset admission, and examine attention across eight layers and five iterations. Section 4.6 adds two case studies testing whether low-scoring synthetic datasets help subsequent online learning.

E5.justification: The new online-RL studies specify five training seeds and standard-error reporting; the rare-success study fixes generated datasets to diffusion seed 0. This adds experiment-specific seed provenance and uncertainty scope. The original three-diffusion-by-five-RL-seed design and 15-seed static baselines are unchanged.

E6.justification: Original result plots are retained, including the three original Figure 6 panels. New results include approximately 55% versus 35% training-pool coverage, RLPD/SAC learning curves, multi-robot iterative outcomes and runtime measurements. Figure 11 reports 80–100% RLPD success within 500,000 interactions versus no SAC success through five million under the newly specified settings.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4.2 adds a runtime model: T_iter = T_diffusion + ceil(N_unsolved/G)(T_gen + T_policy), with serial and fully parallel cases. The original MDP definitions, diffusion mathematics, task-graph formulation and algorithm remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about compositional transition generation and iterative self-improvement are retained. The introduction additionally presents interaction efficiency, usefulness of low-success synthetic datasets and larger-scale validation as empirical contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations of learning stability, reliable dataset coverage, downstream adaptation and scaling. Section 3.3 replaces the model-collapse protection claim with a narrower explanation about localized updates. The conclusion explicitly addresses state-based inputs, unavailable real-world validation, privileged-policy applications and the need for visual extensions.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.3 and Tables 6–7 specify online-RL architectures, ensembles, update ratios, replay mixtures and optimization settings. Appendix A.4 and Table 8 add A6000 runtime measurements and task-level scheduling information. The first-page access instruction changes from a direct repository link to a project website advertising code and visualizations.

R1.justification: v4 adds Ball et al. (2023) for RLPD and removes Shumailov et al. (2024) alongside the model-collapse discussion. Related work more explicitly distinguishes Gao et al., Dream to Manipulate and RoboDreamer from inter-task transition generation, and identifies SynthER as the closest approach. The broader positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition remains verbatim. Local revisions affect the introduction, related work, conclusion and acknowledgments. The low-data justification moves from Appendix A to Section 4.7.1, and the implementation appendix is reorganized around additional experiments and computational costs.

P2.justification: Figure 6 expands from three to five panels. v4 adds a multilayer attention grid, online-learning and scaling figures, and three hyperparameter/runtime tables. The old Figure 9 becomes Figure 12 in the main text; task illustrations are relocated and resized, and the task table becomes Table 9.

improvement.justification: Raw-iteration curves and multi-robot iterative results strengthen v1’s evidence, while runtime measurements and explicit applicability limits improve transparency. However, Section 4.5’s claimed 20,000 interactions are not reconciled with the repeated evaluations specified in Section 4.1 and Table 3. The rare-success comparison also changes both algorithm and offline-data access (Table 7). These weaknesses temper the added practical claims, leaving a modest net improvement.
